before: When your nervous system is flooded, your protective parts are busy with the flood, so they're not going to let your little one come out and talk much anyway. Some people go straight into EMDR on their worst memory before they can even stay in the room. Then they get flooded all over again and decide EMDR doesn't work. Here's a map of what to try when:
after:
### Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over

Pema Chödrön calls the tightening and urge you get before the story has finished forming "shenpa," and she says "hooked" is a more descriptive translation than the usual "attachment." You might notice the hook before you have any clue what part of you is doing the hooking.
guide_passage:
The r4 guide's passage (the passage this carries):
Do not use pleasantness as the only safety meter either. Learning often includes grief, fear, frustration, difficult dreams, or material you would rather not meet. Difficulty by itself is not harm, just as intensity by itself is not progress. But “I stayed oriented” is not enough by itself either. Ask four things: could you stop and return, do you actually want to go back toward it, did it feel difficult-but-workable rather than simply too much or unwanted, and how did you recover afterward in sleep and ordinary functioning?

If those answers are not known yet, do not rush to classify the experience as healing or harmful. Ask how it landed and how you have been since. Then scaffold the challenge. When you are calibrating, changing one thing at a time can teach you what matters; if distress is climbing, change several things at once. Try shorter duration, less depth or imagery, better timing, more symbolic or indirect representation, eyes open or stronger external anchors, less isolation, and more support. Restore challenge gradually only when you want to continue and recovery supports it. This is not throwing yourself into a cauldron to toughen up; it is finding the edge where you can actually learn.

Dreams and imagery can be useful material about what feels important, frightening, missing, or needed now. They are not evidence that the pictured event happened historically. Do not use them to confirm, suggest, or reconstruct a memory.

Teaching points Joel approved (my wording, his yes on 2026-10-09 02:06), with what the article already says:
- T4: How pleasant a session felt doesn't tell you whether it was too much. Hard isn't harm, and staying present isn't enough by itself. (Already in the article: intensity isn't progress, in Joel's crying story at the start.)
- T5: What tells you more: the next few days (sleep, getting through the day), whether you want to go back toward it, and whether it felt hard but workable or just too much. (Whether it helped is already When to Change the Strategy's point; new here is whether it was too much.)
- T6: If you can't tell yet, don't call it healing or harm. Make the next one a bit easier, one change at a time. If you're getting worse, change several things and get support. Bring the challenge back gradually.
- T7: Dreams and images show what feels important or needed now. They aren't evidence that something happened, and they shouldn't be used to build a memory. (Already in the article, for memories in an altered state: "They can feel totally real, but that alone doesn't prove they happened." New here: dreams and session imagery.)

provenance.why_reader_needs_it: Teaching points T4 to T7, which Joel approved on 2026-10-09: how to tell whether a session was too much (not by how pleasant it was; by the next few days, wanting to go back, hard-but-doable or too much), what to do while you can't tell yet, and what dreams and images are and aren't. The article says intensity isn't progress and asks whether a practice helps, but never how to tell a hard session from a harmful one, which is what someone using the somatic map right before this needs.
